consensus_summary: Sin is primarily transgression of God’s law, rebellion against God, and missing His standard—both as wrongful acts and as a fallen condition—producing guilt, alienation, and death, with complementary metaphors (power, debt, stain, sickness) rather than rival definitions.
book_summary: Sin is defined strictly as the transgression of the law, per Scripture’s own wording, with no law implying no transgression and the law giving the knowledge of sin; opposite is righteousness.
consensus_core_identification: Sin = offense against God by transgressing His law / rebelling / missing His mark.
book_core_identification: Sin = the transgression of the law.
boundary_disagreement: None material; the book simply states the legal definition without elaborating condition, power, debt, or therapeutic metaphors that consensus treats as complementary aspects rather than competing cores.
rationale: Reduced cores are the same referent: both identify sin as law-transgression (1 John 3:4 and related texts). Consensus wording adds rebellion, hamartia, and act-plus-condition framing, and lists metaphors as alternatives; the book’s minimal ‘Scripture’s own definition’ is not a replacement or boundary rejection of that core, only a tighter statement of the settled primary sense. Extra consensus detail is immaterial to the identification.
strongest_objection: The book’s silence on original-sin condition and personified-power senses could be read as an implicit narrowing, yet those remain extensions/aspects of the same core rather than a different identification.
